-**MetaDescription**: A comprehensive guide for developers building MCP servers that work with Visual Studio Code.
-
-# MCP developer guide
-
-Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI models to interact with external tools and services through a unified interface. Visual Studio Code implements the full MCP specification, enabling you to create MCP servers that provide tools, prompts, and resources for extending the capabilities of AI agents in VS Code.
-
-MCP servers provide one of three types of tools available in VS Code, alongside built-in tools and extension-contributed tools. Learn more about [tool types](/docs/agents/concepts/tools.md#types-of-tools).
-
-This guide covers everything you need to know to build MCP servers that work seamlessly with VS Code and other MCP clients.
+**MetaDescription**: Integrate MCP servers with Copilot across compatible clients, with configuration and editor guidance.
+
+# Integrate MCP servers with Copilot
+
+This reference helps Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and plugin authors integrate their tools with Copilot in VS Code. It covers configuration, supported capabilities, and editor-specific integrations.
+
+The [Copilot harness](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#copilot) uses the [copilot.copilot_sdk_short], the shared agent runtime used by VS Code, [GitHub Copilot CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-mcp-servers), and the [GitHub Copilot app](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-copilot-app/customize-github-copilot-app#configuring-mcp-servers). Building for its MCP support makes the same server usable across these compatible Copilot experiences, not only in the editor. Your server implements MCP and doesn't need to depend on the [copilot.copilot_sdk_short].
+
+* **Make your server available:** choose a [delivery method](#make-your-server-available-to-copilot).
+* **Check compatibility:** review [Copilot capability support](#mcp-support-in-copilot) and connected-client requirements.
+* **Maintain an existing Local integration:** expand the [deprecated Local compatibility appendix](#local-harness-compatibility-deprecated) `feature(local-harness)`.
+
+For protocol and server implementation guidance, use the [MCP documentation and SDKs](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/sdk).
 
 > [!TIP]
 > For information about using MCP servers as an end user, see [Use MCP servers in VS Code](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md).
 
-## Why use MCP servers?
-
-Implementing an MCP server to extend chat in VS Code with language model tools has the following benefits:
-
-- **Extend agent mode** with specialized, domain-specific, tools that are automatically invoked as part of responding to a user prompt. For example, enable database scaffolding and querying to dynamically provide the LLM with relevant context.
-- **Flexible deployment options** for local and remote scenarios.
-- **Reuse** your MCP server across different tools and platforms.
-
-You might consider implementing a language model tool with the [Language Model API](/api/extension-guides/ai/tools) in the following scenarios:
-
-- You want to deeply integrate with VS Code by using extension APIs.
-- You want to distribute your tool and updates by using the Visual Studio Marketplace.
-
-## MCP features supported by VS Code
-
-VS Code supports the following MCP capabilities:
-
-* [Transports](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports):
-    * Local standard input/output (`stdio`)
-    * Streamable HTTP (`http`)
-    * Server-sent events (`sse`) - legacy support.
-
-* [Features](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18#features):
-    * Tools: extend [agent mode](/docs/chat/chat-overview) with extra tools
-    * Prompts: add reusable prompts as slash commands in chat
-    * Resources: provide data and content that users can add as chat context or interact with directly in VS Code
-    * Elicitation: request input from the user
-    * Sampling: make language model requests using the user's configured models and subscription
-    * Authentication: authorize access to an MCP server using OAuth
-    * Server instructions
-    * Roots: provide information about the user's workspace root folder(s)
-    * [MCP Apps](https://modelcontextprotocol.github.io/ext-apps/api/): return interactive UI components from tools
+## Make your server available to Copilot
+
+Use a managed connection for a supported service, or distribute your own server configuration or integration:
+
+| Delivery method | When to use it |
+|-----------------|----------------|
+| **Copilot connector** `feature(copilot-connectors)` | Use a [[product.prodname_github]-managed MCP connection](/docs/agent-customization/copilot-connectors.md) for a supported service. [product.prodname_github] handles configuration and authentication, with no local server setup. |
+| **Native configuration** | Provide a launch command or HTTP endpoint that compatible Copilot clients can use without an editor extension. |
+| **Agent plugin** | [Bundle the server with skills and other customizations](/docs/agents/reference/agent-plugin-reference.md#mcp-servers-in-plugins) for a reusable workflow. Servers load through the plugin, not as copies in an editor profile. |
+| **Connected-editor integration** | Offer an [installation URL](#create-an-mcp-installation-or-lookup-url) or [register the server from an extension](#register-an-mcp-server-in-your-extension). Eligible editor-provided definitions can be forwarded to the runtime. |
+
+Connectors reuse the managed connection across supported Copilot clients signed in with the same account. For self-managed servers, prefer native configuration or an agent plugin for cross-client reuse. Each execution host needs the required dependencies, credentials, and service access. Editor-dependent features don't automatically transfer to another client.
+
+### Native configuration
+
+In VS Code, users add servers through **Chat: Open Customizations** > **MCP Servers** > **Add Server**. **Global** > **Copilot Global** selects the native user configuration. Link your installation instructions to the [connection walkthrough](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md#add-a-server-by-url-or-command).
+
+For manual configuration, provide an entry using the portable `mcpServers` format. This example connects to an HTTP server:
+
+```json
+{
+    "mcpServers": {
+        "myService": {
+            "type": "http",
+            "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
+            "tools": ["*"]
+        }
+    }
+}
+```
+
+Replace the example URL with your server's MCP endpoint and document any authentication requirements. Don't include credentials in shared configuration.
+
+The harness reads native configuration directly on the host where it runs:
+
+* **Workspace:** `.mcp.json` at the workspace root.
+* **User:** `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json`, or `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` when `COPILOT_HOME` is unset.
+
+For stdio commands, supported fields, secrets, and remote hosts, see the [MCP configuration reference](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md). Don't use the deprecated Local `servers` format for new native configurations.
+
+Before distributing an integration, [verify an actual tool call](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md#verify-the-first-tool-call) in the intended Copilot experience. Adding configuration alone doesn't confirm that the session can use its tools. For failures, see [MCP troubleshooting](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md#troubleshoot-mcp-servers).
+
+## MCP support in Copilot
+
+Start with tools, then add capabilities that your integration needs. Support depends on both the Copilot harness that runs the session and the client that presents it. Some capabilities require a connected client, such as the editor that renders MCP Apps or handles authentication.
+
+| Capability | Support and limitations in Copilot |
+|------------|------------------------------------|
+| [Tools](#tools) | Invokes server tools under the session's tool availability and approval policies. |
+| [Sampling](#sampling) | Deprecated in MCP. Supported on compatible connections during an active turn, with per-server approval. |
+| [Elicitation](#elicitation) | Presents form and URL requests through host-rendered input during an active turn. |
+| [MCP Apps](#mcp-apps) | Displays interactive tool UI in a connected client that renders MCP Apps. This integration is Experimental. |
+| [Authorization](#authorization) | Supports MCP OAuth with authentication handled by the connected client. |
+| [Resources](#resources) | Reads resources for MCP Apps. Native servers don't automatically appear in the editor's resource browser. |
+| [Roots](#workspace-roots) | Deprecated in MCP. Existing integrations must check the runtime's negotiated capability and returned roots. |
+| [Prompts](#prompts) | The editor's `/mcp.<server>.<prompt>` completion flow isn't exposed in Copilot sessions. Use skills to distribute reusable workflows. |
+
+This table describes available integrations, not full MCP specification conformance. Check the capabilities negotiated with the target client and match your implementation to the [SDK's protocol-version guidance](https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/protocol-versions). Sampling and roots are [deprecated in MCP 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/deprecated), so prefer their alternatives for new integrations.
+
```

+## Where skills come from
+
+Skills can come from the following sources:
+
+* **Project or personal files:** [Create a skill](#create-a-skill), [copy and adapt one](#copy-and-adapt-an-existing-skill), or use skills included in a repository.
+* **Marketplaces and plugins:** [Install individual skills](#install-a-skill-from-the-customization-marketplace-preview) or use skills bundled in an [agent plugin](/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins.md).
+* **Extensions:** Installed VS Code extensions can [contribute skills](#contribute-skills-from-extensions).
+* **MCP servers:** Connected servers can [supply skills](#use-skills-from-an-mcp-server) `feature(mcp-skills)` for Copilot harness sessions.
+
+Supported sources depend on your [agent harness](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md). For project and personal skill directories, see [Skill locations](#skill-locations).
+
 ## Use an existing skill
 
 Start with an existing skill when it provides the workflow you need. [Browse customization marketplaces](/docs/agent-customization/overview.md#discover-and-install-existing-customizations-preview) to install an individual skill or find one bundled in an [agent plugin](/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins.md). You can also copy and adapt a skill for your project. Review the requirements for [reusing customizations across harnesses](/docs/agent-customization/overview.md#reuse-customizations-across-harnesses) before choosing a source and location.
@@ -72,6 +83,32 @@
 
 For source availability and setup, see [Discover and install existing customizations](/docs/agent-customization/overview.md#discover-and-install-existing-customizations-preview).
 
+### Use skills from an MCP server
+
+`feature(mcp-skills)`
+
+An [MCP server](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md) can provide Agent Skills alongside its tools. These skills supply reusable instructions for working with a service, without requiring you to copy a skill directory into your project. This feature requires the [Copilot harness](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#copilot) and isn't available in Local harness sessions `feature(local-harness)`.
+
+1. Enable the ``chat.agentHost.mcpSkills.enabled`` setting. It is off by default.
+1. [Add an MCP server](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md#add-a-server-by-url-or-command) that provides skills, following the publisher's setup instructions.
+1. Start a new session with the Copilot harness. Changing the setting doesn't affect sessions that are already running.
+1. Ask the agent to describe the skills available from that server.
+1. With that session selected, run **Chat: Open Customizations** and select **Skills**. Server-provided skills appear under **Skills from \<server\>**. Open a skill to inspect its read-only instructions.
+1. In chat, type `/` and select a skill, shown as `/<server>:<skill>`, or ask the agent to use it.
+
+Before the agent loads instructions from a server, it asks **Allow Skills from \<server\>?**. Only allow instructions from servers you trust. Your choice applies to that server:
+
+| Choice | Effect |
+|--------|--------|
+| **Allow Once** | Allow skills for the current session, including later turns. A new session asks again. |
+| **Always Allow** | Allow skills in the current and future sessions, including after a reload. |
+| **Not Now** | Decline for the current turn. A later turn can ask again. |
+| **Never** | Decline in the current and future sessions, including after a reload. |
+

-Add an MCP server when your agent needs a capability its existing tools don't provide, such as querying a database or retrieving information from an external service. +Choose how to add the capability you need:
 
-This article takes you from adding a server to verifying its first tool call. Choose your starting point:
-
-* **Connect a supported service without server setup:** [Use a Copilot connector](/docs/agent-customization/copilot-connectors.md) `feature(copilot-connectors)`.
-* **Use tools from a packaged workflow:** [Install an agent plugin](/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins.md#discover-and-install-plugins) that bundles MCP servers.
-* **I have a server URL or command:** [Connect a server](#connect-a-server).
-* **Help me find a server:** [Choose a server to try](#choose-a-server-to-try) or [browse the Customization Marketplace](#discover-servers-in-the-customization-marketplace-preview).
-* **My server is configured but isn't working:** [Check the connection](#if-the-server-does-not-work).
+* **Connect a supported service:** use a [Copilot connector](/docs/agent-customization/copilot-connectors.md) `feature(copilot-connectors)`. [product.prodname_github] manages configuration and authentication without local server setup.
+* **Find a published integration:** [browse servers](#find-and-install-a-server) or [install an agent plugin](/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins.md#discover-and-install-plugins) that bundles MCP tools.
+* **Add a server directly:** [use a publisher's URL or launch command](#add-a-server-by-url-or-command).
 
 ## Before you start
 
 * [Enable AI features](/docs/getstarted/overview.md#enable-ai-features) and open a local project folder in VS Code.
-* Select the intended harness in the **Session Target** dropdown. The walkthrough below uses **Copilot** and a personal configuration. Choose a different destination below if you need to share the server or use a Local harness configuration.
-* For manually configured servers, check the server publisher's prerequisites. A remote HTTP server can require an account or sign-in. A server launched by a command needs its runtime installed on the machine that runs it.
+* Select **Copilot** in the **Session Target** dropdown. The connection example below uses a personal configuration.
 
 > [!CAUTION]
-> Local MCP servers can run code on your machine, and tools can access external services using your permissions. Review the publisher, command or endpoint, and requested access before installing or starting a server. Only trust configurations you have reviewed. Learn about [MCP server trust](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md#mcp-server-trust).
+> Local MCP servers can run code on your machine, and tools can access services using your permissions. Review the publisher, command or endpoint, and requested access before installing or starting a server. Learn about [MCP server trust](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md#mcp-server-trust).
 
-## Choose a configuration destination
-
-Choose a destination before adding the server so its tools are available to the intended harness and users:
-
-| Your goal | Configuration |
-|-----------|---------------|
-| Use a server across your workspaces | **Global** > **Copilot Global** writes to `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json`, or `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` when `COPILOT_HOME` is unset. |
-| Share a server with a team using compatible Copilot tools | Workspace-root `.mcp.json`. The guided flow offers this destination when the Experimental ``chat.mcp.workspaceRootConfig.enabled`` setting is on. |
-| Use a Local harness configuration with input variables or per-server sandboxing | Workspace `.vscode/mcp.json` or user-profile `mcp.json`. These destinations remain available for compatibility and are labeled deprecated in the guided flow. |
-
-Portable files use a top-level `mcpServers` object. The VS Code format uses `servers`. Don't copy a configuration between them without checking the [format and capability reference](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md#configuration-file).
-
-> [!IMPORTANT]
-> Portable configurations don't support VS Code input variables or environment files. Servers requiring interactive inputs aren't forwarded to Copilot harness sessions. Use the [authentication guidance for your configuration](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md#authentication-and-secrets), rather than adding unsupported credential placeholders.
-
-For [Dev Containers](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md#remote-workspaces-and-dev-containers) or [command-line installation](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md#command-line-installation), follow the environment-specific instructions.
-
-## Choose a server to try
-
-For a concrete local example, use the [Playwright MCP server](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp). It requires **Node.js 18 or newer**, with `npx` available. Check your installation in a terminal:
-
-```bash
-node --version
-npx --version
-```
-
-The walkthrough uses Playwright to demonstrate connecting an external tool provider. For everyday browser interaction, try the [built-in browser tools](/docs/agents/run/browser-tools.md) first: they don't require an MCP server.
-
-To try a remote documentation server instead, follow the [Context7 setup requirements](https://context7.com/docs/resources/all-clients) for its current authentication requirements and service limits. Use the HTTP endpoint `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp` in the connection steps below. A remote server doesn't require a local Node.js installation.
-
-## Connect a server
-
-Use the publisher's URL or launch command. For the Playwright example, use the command in step two.
-
-1. With the intended harness selected, run **Chat: Open Customizations** from the Command Palette (``Shortcut: workbench.action.showCommands``) and select **MCP Servers**. Select **Add Server** (**+**) in the **User** or **Workspace** group for your chosen scope.
-
-1. Choose the option that matches what the publisher provides:
-
-    | What you have | Choose | Enter |
-    |---------------|--------|-------|
-    | A server URL | **HTTP (HTTP or Server-Sent Events)** | The publisher's MCP endpoint. |
-    | A launch command | **Command (stdio)** | The command and its arguments. The server communicates through standard input and output. |
-
-    For Playwright, choose **Command (stdio)** and enter:
-
-    ```bash
-    npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest
-    ```
-
-1. Enter a server ID, such as `playwright` or `context7`, that isn't already used in the destination configuration. Use distinct IDs for different servers you plan to use together.
-
-1. For a personal configuration, select **Global**, and then **Copilot Global** when prompted. This stores the server outside your project. For team configurations or other harnesses, [choose a configuration destination](#choose-a-configuration-destination).
-
-    If **Copilot Global** isn't available, check the [Copilot harness requirements](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#copilot) before continuing with this walkthrough.
-
-1. Review any server trust or authentication prompts before accepting them. Follow the publisher's sign-in instructions if the service requires authentication. Do not paste credentials into chat or commit them to your project.
-
-As an alternative to the Agent Customizations editor, run **MCP: Add Server** from the Command Palette to start the guided flow. Follow any prompts to select the destination for your harness.
-
-For other ways to add a server, see [Find another server](#find-another-server).
-
-## Verify the first tool call
-
-Adding a configuration isn't proof that the agent can use the server. Complete a request and inspect the tool call:
-
-1. In the agent session, enter a prompt that explicitly names the server and a low-impact action. For Playwright:
-
-    ```prompt
-    Use the Playwright MCP server to open <your URL here> and report the page title. Use its tools, not the built-in browser tools. Do not change files.
-    ```
-
-    For Context7:
-
-    ```prompt
-    Use the Context7 MCP tools to look up the React documentation for useState. Summarize the basic usage and cite the documentation returned by the tool. Do not change files.
-    ```
-
-1. Review startup, sign-in, and tool approval requests as they appear. Approve only actions you understand.
-
-1. Expand the tool call in the conversation. Check that it belongs to the server you added and inspect its returned output.
-
-**Your connection works when all three checks pass:**
-
```

-## Frequently asked questions
-
-### Can I keep using the Local harness while adapting my customizations?
-
-Yes, when organization controls permit it. In the editor's Chat view, start a new session and select **Local** as the **Session Target**. Local harness availability and automatic Copilot harness selection depend on your settings and organization policies. See [Keep the Local harness available while migrating](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#can-i-keep-local-available-while-migrating).
-
-Administrators can use the temporary `vscode.temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness` enterprise-managed setting, available from version 1.142. It keeps the Local harness available and suppresses automatic Copilot routing, but the Local harness does not enforce Copilot runtime-only sandbox and permission rules. It does not override `vscode.temporaryAllowLocalHarness: false`, available from version 1.143. Review the [administrator guidance and security caveat](/docs/enterprise/manage-ai-settings.md#keep-local-harness-as-default).
-
-### Why are MCP servers with input prompts missing?
-
-Servers that require `${input:...}` or `${command:...}` variables are not forwarded from `.vscode/mcp.json` or profile `mcp.json` to the Copilot harness. The server's tools are therefore unavailable in the session. Resolving the prompt in a Local session first does not help: Copilot forwarding rejects these variables before resolving their values, including cached values.
-
-Moving the same configuration to `.mcp.json` does not add input-prompt support. Migration converts eligible non-secret inputs to environment variables. For password inputs or other manual changes, see [Replace input prompts with environment variables](#replace-input-prompts-with-environment-variables). Keep the original configuration until you have a supported authentication method and have verified the tools in a Copilot session. See [MCP input variables](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md#input-variables-for-sensitive-data) and the open reports [microsoft/vscode#334271](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/334271) and [microsoft/vscode#337311](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/337311).
-
-### Can Copilot pass a prompted secret to an HTTP MCP server without an environment variable or a file?
-
-There is no built-in MCP configuration option that passes a VS Code `${input:...}` value or reads an existing `SecretStorage` value into an HTTP server's authentication header for the Copilot harness. Setting `password: true` on an input does not change this limitation.
-
-If the server supports OAuth, use its supported authorization flow instead of configuring a static bearer token. OAuth is a separate authentication mechanism, not a way to forward a prompted API key. Authentication UI gaps are tracked in [microsoft/vscode#339960](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/339960).
-
-If the server requires a fixed bearer token and your requirements exclude both environment variables and credentials in files, the Copilot harness has no equivalent built-in input-prompt workflow. Continue using Local for that integration while you evaluate supported authentication options. Do not replace the placeholder with a literal secret in either a shared or personal MCP file: personal files can also be read by tools and included in logs or other artifacts. See [Authentication and secrets](/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration.md#authentication-and-secrets).
-
```

 # Understand context in AI agents

 Conversation history is scoped to a chat and isn't automatically shared with other chats or sessions. Persistent sources, such as [custom instructions](/docs/agent-customization/custom-instructions.md) or [agent memory](/docs/agents/concepts/agents.md#memory), can also provide information across conversations.
 
+## Context, knowledge, and memory
+
+Several sources help an agent respond, but they have different lifetimes:
+
+| Source | What it provides | What persists |
+|--------|------------------|---------------|
+| **Model training** | General capabilities and knowledge learned before your request. | The model's trained knowledge is separate from your chat. It doesn't automatically include your project. |
+| **Current context** | Information included in a particular model request, such as your message, files, and tool results. | Later requests need to include that information again, or retrieve it when needed. |
+| **Conversation history** | The discussion and tool activity in the current chat. | Saved history can outlast a request, but the model only sees the portion included in its context, which can be summarized. Other chats don't automatically inherit it. |
+| **Custom instructions** | Reusable guidance, such as project conventions and test commands. | Instructions remain in their configured source and apply when the harness discovers and includes them. |
+| **Memory** | Selected preferences or project facts stored separately from the conversation. | Retention and sharing depend on the memory system. A saved fact must be retrieved to inform a response. |
+
+Adding context is not the same as training a model. Correcting an answer can guide later responses while that correction remains in context, but doesn't by itself update the trained model or establish memory in other chats. Separate provider policies govern data retention and use for training. See [where information goes](/docs/agents/concepts/trust-and-safety.md#where-information-goes).
+
+For example, put a required project test command in [custom instructions](/docs/agent-customization/custom-instructions.md) rather than relying on an earlier chat. Use [memory](/docs/agents/run/memory.md) for supported preferences and reusable facts, and review saved information for accuracy.
+
 ## How VS Code assembles context
 
 Each time the agent sends a request to the language model, VS Code assembles a prompt from multiple sources:

 # Understand language models
 
-Visual Studio Code uses large language models (LLMs) to power its AI features. You have flexibility in which models you use and how you access them:
+Visual Studio Code uses large language models (LLMs) to power its AI features. A model interprets the information provided to it and generates a response, such as an explanation, code, or a request to use a tool.
 
-* **Models from your GitHub Copilot plan**: choose from multiple models by different providers, such as Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, included with your plan.
-* **Other accounts**: use an [account supported by the selected harness](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#cloud-target), such as a ChatGPT account for Codex. Model availability, usage limits, and billing depend on that account's plan and the harness.
-* **Bring your own key (BYOK)**: add models from other providers with your own API key, or host your own models, including local models that run offline. With BYOK, you can use agents in VS Code without a GitHub Copilot plan.
-* **On-device models** `feature(on-device-models)`: download a [Copilot-provided coding model](/docs/agent-customization/language-models.md#use-on-device-models-experimental) and run it on a supported NVIDIA GPU in Copilot harness sessions.
-
-> [!NOTE]
-> Claude and Codex harnesses are disabled when [Copilot enterprise-managed settings apply](/docs/enterprise/manage-ai-settings.md#claude-and-codex-availability), even when you use separate provider credentials. Contact the IT team that deployed the settings to discuss access. This harness restriction does not itself disable Claude or OpenAI models in the Copilot harness.
-
-This article explains how language models work, their characteristics, and when to select a model, use Auto, or use Copilot Fusion.
-
-![Screenshot of the Language Models editor, showing the list of available models.](../images/language-models/language-models-editor.png)
+This article explains what models can and can't do, how tokens and context limits affect your work, and how to balance quality, speed, and cost when choosing a model. For setup steps, see [choose and configure language models](/docs/agent-customization/language-models.md).
 
 ## How language models work
 
-A language model processes text input (a "prompt") and generates text output. In VS Code, the prompt is assembled from multiple sources: your message, conversation history, file contents, tool outputs, and custom instructions. The model generates responses that can include explanations, code edits, or requests to call [tools](/docs/agents/concepts/tools.md).
+A language model generates a response based on patterns learned during training and the information in its current input, or **prompt**. In VS Code, the full prompt includes more than the message you type: it can contain conversation history, file contents, tool outputs, and custom instructions. Some models also accept images and other input formats.
 
 Language models don't execute code or access files directly. Instead, they generate text that the [agent loop](/docs/agents/concepts/agents.md#agent-loop) interprets as actions. When a model requests a tool call, VS Code executes the tool and feeds the result back to the model for the next iteration.
 
 Some key characteristics of language models include:
 
-* **Nondeterministic**: the same prompt can produce different results each time. This is by design and reflects how the model samples from probability distributions.
+* **Nondeterministic**: the same prompt can produce different results. A successful response once doesn't guarantee the same result on another attempt.
 * **Context-dependent**: the quality of the response depends on the quality and relevance of the [context](/docs/agents/concepts/context.md) provided in the prompt.
-* **Knowledge boundaries**: models are trained on data up to a certain date and might produce outdated or incorrect information for topics beyond their training data. VS Code mitigates this with tools and workspace indexing.
+* **Limited training knowledge**: training doesn't automatically include your current codebase or the latest API changes. Tools can retrieve current information for the model to use.
+* **Fallible**: a model can produce a confident but incorrect answer, sometimes called a hallucination, even about familiar topics or code it has read. Tool results help ground an answer in evidence, but don't guarantee correctness.
+
+Review explanations against their sources and validate generated code. A convincing response or a detailed reasoning summary is not a substitute for checking the result.
+
+## Tokens
+
+Models process text in units called **tokens**. A token can represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another piece of text. Token counts are not the same as word or character counts and vary by model.
+
+Input tokens represent information sent to the model. Output tokens represent what it generates. Tokens help measure both the model's [context limits](#context-window) and the [cost of requests](#ai-credits-and-model-costs).
+
+One user request can trigger many model requests as the agent reads files, calls tools, and checks results. Each step can process additional tokens.
 
 ## Context window
 
-The context window is the total amount of information a model can process in a single request. It includes everything: the system prompt, custom instructions, conversation history, file contents, tool outputs, and your current message. Different models have different context window sizes.
+The context window is the amount of information a model can process in a single request, measured in tokens. Instructions, conversation history, file contents, tool outputs, and your message consume that budget, and room is also needed for the response. The available input and output limits depend on the model.
 
-When the context window fills up, VS Code automatically summarizes older parts of the conversation to make room. This means important details from early in a long conversation might be compressed or lost. You can also type `/compact` in the chat input to manually trigger compaction at any time. Optionally, add custom instructions after the command to guide the summary, for example `/compact focus on the API design decisions`.
+A larger window can accommodate more information, but doesn't automatically include your whole repository or guarantee that the model uses every detail correctly. Focused, relevant context still matters.
+
+As a conversation approaches its limit, supported harnesses compact older content into a summary to make room. Details can be compressed or omitted, so a long conversation is not a perfect record of everything the model can still use.
 
 Learn more about [how VS Code assembles context](/docs/agents/concepts/context.md) and [context compaction](/docs/agents/run/sessions/manage-sessions.md#compact-conversation-context).
 
 ## Thinking and reasoning
 
-Some language models can perform extended reasoning, also called "thinking", before producing a response. Instead of generating an answer immediately, a reasoning model first works through the problem internally, considering multiple approaches, evaluating trade-offs, and building a step-by-step chain of thought. This internal reasoning happens in dedicated thinking tokens that are separate from the final output.
+Some models use additional computation, often called **thinking** or **reasoning**, before producing a response. This can help with tasks that require comparing approaches or working through several dependent steps.
 
-Reasoning models are especially effective for complex tasks like multi-step debugging, architectural planning, code refactoring, and mathematical or scientific analysis. For simpler tasks like generating boilerplate or answering basic questions, the extra reasoning adds latency without significant benefit.
+Reasoning can be useful for multi-step debugging, architectural planning, and complex refactoring. For a small edit or straightforward question, extra reasoning might add time and cost without improving the result. It does not remove the need for review.
 
 ### Thinking effort
 
-Thinking effort controls how much reasoning a model applies to each request. Higher effort levels produce more thorough internal reasoning, which improves quality for complex problems. Lower effort levels reduce latency and token usage by limiting or skipping the thinking step.
+Thinking effort controls how much reasoning a supported model can apply to a request. Higher effort can help with complex problems, but is not a guarantee of higher quality. Lower effort can reduce latency and token usage.
 
 The available effort levels and their default values vary by model and provider. Some models also support *adaptive thinking*, where the model dynamically decides whether and how much to reason based on the complexity of each request, rather than always using a fixed thinking budget.
 
@@ -52,9 +55,9 @@
 
 ### Thinking tokens
 
-Thinking tokens count toward the model's context window, even though they are not visible in the response. The actual thinking output is typically returned in summarized form or can be omitted entirely for lower latency. Keep in mind that higher thinking effort levels can produce more thinking tokens, which can increase latency.
+Models that use thinking tokens spend part of their generation on reasoning rather than the final answer. A visible thinking summary isn't necessarily the full reasoning output. How these tokens affect context limits and billing varies by model and provider.
 
-Learn how to [configure the thinking effort level](/docs/agent-customization/language-models.md#configure-thinking-effort) in VS Code.
+Learn how to [configure the thinking effort level](/docs/agent-customization/language-models.md#configure-thinking-effort-and-context-size) in VS Code.
 
 ## Choose the right model

 * **Reasoning models** excel at complex refactoring, architectural decisions, multi-step debugging, and tasks that require analyzing trade-offs.
-* **Large context models** work well for large codebases or long conversations where retaining more information matters.
+* **Large context models** can accommodate more source material or conversation history. The agent still needs to find and include the relevant information.
 
 You can switch models at any time, based on your needs for a particular task. For a detailed comparison, see [Choosing the right AI model for your task](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/ai-models/choosing-the-right-ai-model-for-your-task) in the GitHub Copilot documentation.
 
 ### Auto model selection
 
-Auto model selection in GitHub Copilot combines two systems to select one model for each request. One system tracks real-time model health and availability, while the other evaluates task complexity. Together, they match each task to the model that can solve it most efficiently, reserving higher-cost reasoning models for problems that need them and routing simpler tasks to faster models.
+Auto model selection in GitHub Copilot selects a model for each request based on task complexity and model availability. Use Auto when you want the service to make that choice rather than selecting a model yourself.
 
 In [Copilot harness sessions](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#copilot), the same routing entry can appear as **Copilot Fusion** instead of **Auto**, depending on your settings and the tiers offered to your account. Fusion adds [multi-model orchestration](#copilot-fusion) alongside single-model routing.
 
 Auto selects from multiple models and respects your organization's [model access settings](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-ai-models/configure-access-to-ai-models). Auto won't select models excluded by administrator policies or models restricted by data-residency policies.
-
-When you turn on **Use in Auto** for an [on-device model](/docs/agent-customization/language-models.md#use-on-device-models-experimental), Auto can route some requests to that model on your device, with cloud fallback.
 
 For more details, see [About Copilot auto model selection](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/auto-model-selection) in the GitHub documentation.
 
@@ -88,35 +89,29 @@
 
 ### AI credits and model costs
 
-Each Copilot plan includes a monthly allowance of [AI credits](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/billing/usage-based-billing-for-individuals). Different models consume AI credits at different rates, based on the model and the number of tokens processed. More capable models cost more per token, while lighter models extend your usage further. When you use auto model selection, VS Code routes each request to an efficient model that balances quality and cost.
+GitHub Copilot plans use [AI credits](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/billing/usage-based-billing-for-individuals) to measure usage. Consumption depends on the model's rates and the tokens processed, not only the number of messages you send. Check your plan for its allowance and usage limits.
 
 Copilot Fusion can use multiple model passes for a task, such as drafting, critique, and revision. Each pass contributes to AI credit consumption, so an orchestrated workflow can take longer and use more credits than a single-model request.

 VS Code supports three types of tools:
 
-* **Built-in tools**: tools that ship with VS Code for common development tasks, like reading and writing files, running terminal commands, searching your codebase, and navigating the editor. These are available immediately without any setup.
+* **Built-in tools**: tools supplied for common development tasks, like reading and writing files, running terminal commands, and searching your codebase. Which tools are available depends on the harness and interface.
 * **MCP tools**: tools provided by [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) servers, an open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources. MCP tools can come from servers you [configure directly](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md), managed [Copilot connectors](/docs/agent-customization/copilot-connectors.md) `feature(copilot-connectors)`, or servers bundled in [agent plugins](/docs/agent-customization/agent-plugins.md). MCP servers can run locally on your machine or be hosted remotely. Use MCP tools to connect to databases, APIs, and other external services.
 * **Extension tools**: tools contributed by VS Code extensions through the Language Model Tools API. Extension tools integrate deeply with the editor and are available when you install the extension.
+
+An MCP server can also supply [skills](/docs/agent-customization/agent-skills.md#use-skills-from-an-mcp-server) `feature(mcp-skills)` in Copilot harness sessions: tools provide actions the agent can take, while skills provide workflow instructions.

-**MetaDescription**: Understand approvals, review, sandboxing, and security considerations for AI agents in VS Code.
+**MetaDescription**: Understand AI limitations, data handling, approvals, and isolation in VS Code.
 
 # Understand trust and safety for AI agents
 
-AI-generated output requires review. Visual Studio Code includes multiple mechanisms to keep you in control of what changes reach your codebase. This article explains the control mechanisms, AI limitations, and security considerations you should be aware of.
+Agents can change files and act on external systems, so using them requires more than checking the final answer. Visual Studio Code provides controls for limiting actions and reviewing results.
+
+This article explains AI limitations, where information goes, and how approvals, trust, and isolation work together. Use it to understand the protections you need before following the [security setup guidance](/docs/agents/run/security.md).

+

+Working on local files doesn't necessarily mean AI processing stays on your machine. Consider three separate flows:

 ## MCP servers in plugins
 
-Plugins can bundle [MCP servers](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md) to provide agents with additional tools and data sources. Plugin MCP servers start automatically when the plugin is enabled and stop when the plugin is disabled.
+Plugins can bundle [MCP servers](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md) to provide agents with additional tools and data sources. In Copilot sessions, these servers are delivered with the plugin rather than forwarded as separate editor-managed definitions. Don't copy them into your personal configuration unless you intend to maintain an independent server entry.
+
+Enabling a plugin makes its MCP servers available to the runtime, subject to server enablement, authentication, and policy. Disabling the plugin makes its servers unavailable. Server startup and available capabilities depend on the harness and client; see [MCP support and limitations](/api/extension-guides/ai/mcp.md#mcp-support-in-copilot).
 
 ### MCP configuration file
 
@@ -268,15 +270,13 @@
 
 ### How plugin MCP servers interact with other servers
 
-Plugin MCP servers appear alongside workspace and user-level MCP servers. You can manage them through the same tools:
-
-* Select **Configure Tools** in the Chat view to see tools from all MCP servers, including plugin servers.
-
-* Run **MCP: List Servers** from the Command Palette to view plugin servers alongside other servers.
-
-Plugin MCP servers are implicitly trusted when you install the plugin. Unlike workspace MCP servers, they do not show a separate trust prompt at startup.
-
-Disabling a plugin stops its MCP servers. Tools provided by the stopped servers are no longer available in chat.
+For Copilot sessions, open **Chat: Open Customizations** > **MCP Servers** in the intended session's context. Plugin MCP servers appear alongside native workspace and user servers. Use the server's available actions to control it or inspect output. If the plugin is disabled, **Enable Plugin** enables the plugin, not only that server.
+
+Use [server and tool controls](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md#control-or-remove-a-server) to distinguish stopping a running server, disabling it, and limiting available tools. Tool availability does not bypass host approvals or service authorization.
+
+For the deprecated Local harness `feature(local-harness)`, **Configure Tools** in the chat input selects tools for a request. **MCP: List Servers** provides controls for editor-managed server connections. These controls do not necessarily affect the runtime connection in a Copilot session.
+
+Review the publisher, server commands, endpoints, and permissions before installing a plugin. Installation can make server code available to run; don't rely on a separate server trust prompt as the point at which to review it.
 
 ## Hooks in plugins
 
@@ -287,7 +287,7 @@
 
 Organizations can distribute approved hooks through plugins. When managed settings specify `allowManagedHooksOnly: true`, plugin hooks run only when the plugin is force-enabled by a managed `enabledPlugins["plugin@marketplace"]: true` entry. User enablement alone is not sufficient, and `allowManagedHooksOnly` does not itself enable the plugin. See [Deploy hooks through managed plugins](/docs/enterprise/manage-ai-settings.md#deploy-hooks-through-managed-plugins).
 
-For Copilot sessions, use the [Copilot hooks reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference) for configuration, event payloads, and output decisions. A plugin packages hooks; it does not translate Local scripts into the shared harness's contract.
+For Copilot sessions, use the [Copilot hooks reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference) for configuration, event payloads, and output decisions. A plugin packages hooks; it does not translate Local harness scripts `feature(local-harness)` into the shared harness's contract.
 
 When adopting or updating a plugin, follow [Migrate hooks](/docs/agent-customization/migrate-customizations.md#migrate-hooks). Update the source package, not its installation cache. Check bundled scripts, path references, agent-scoped hooks, and any duplicate commands in user settings or repository hook files.

To reuse profile-based agents with another harness, [move them to that harness's user folder](/docs/agent-customization/migrate-customizations.md#move-user-agents-and-instructions).
 
 Prefer native harness folders, such as `.github/agents` and `~/.copilot/agents`, over custom search locations. The ``chat.agentFilesLocations`` setting remains supported and is not deprecated. -
-MCP server configuration uses one of the following file formats:
-

-Copilot harness sessions read the portable format directly. +
+* **Connect a server to Copilot:** [choose a configuration destination](#configure-mcp-for-copilot), then use the [portable examples and fields](#portable-configuration).
+* **Reuse an existing editor configuration:** check [forwarding and migration](#editor-forwarding-to-copilot).
+* **Maintain a deprecated Local configuration:** use the separate [Local compatibility reference](#editor-managed-configuration-for-local-harness-compatibility).
+
+For a complete first-time walkthrough, see [Add MCP servers](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md). To operate an existing server, see [Manage and troubleshoot MCP servers](/docs/agents/run/manage-mcp-servers.md).
+
+Configuration compatibility is separate from protocol support. For tools, prompts, resources, roots, sampling, elicitation, and MCP Apps, see [MCP support and limitations](/api/extension-guides/ai/mcp.md#mcp-support-in-copilot).
+
+## Configure MCP for Copilot
+
+Use the Agent Customizations editor to add a server to the intended Copilot session:
+
+1. Select the **Copilot** harness in a chat session, then run **Chat: Open Customizations** and select **MCP Servers**.
+
+1. Select **Add Server**, provide the publisher's command or endpoint, and choose a destination below. For personal configuration, select **Global** > **Copilot Global**.
+
+1. Complete any authentication prompts and [verify a tool call](/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers.md#verify-the-first-tool-call). Adding a configuration alone doesn't confirm that the session can use the server.
+
+### Configuration file
+
+Choose a native Copilot destination. Both files use a top-level `mcpServers` object, and the harness reads them directly.
+
+| Your goal | Configuration file | Guided setup destination |
+|-----------|--------------------|--------------------------|
+| Use a server across your workspaces | `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json`, or `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` when `COPILOT_HOME` is unset | **Global** > **Copilot Global** |
+| Share server definitions with your team | `.mcp.json` at the workspace root | Workspace-root `.mcp.json`, offered when the Experimental ``chat.mcp.workspaceRootConfig.enabled`` setting is on |
+
+As an alternative to guided setup, edit the native file using the [portable configuration examples](#portable-configuration). Existing workspace-root `.mcp.json` files remain available when the guided-setup setting is off.
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> For new Copilot configurations, use these native destinations, not `.vscode/mcp.json` or profile `mcp.json`. Those files use the deprecated Local harness's `feature(local-harness)` editor-managed `servers` format. Eligible existing definitions can be [forwarded](#editor-forwarding-to-copilot), but the harness doesn't read those files directly.
+
+[Plugin-provided servers](/docs/agents/reference/agent-plugin-reference.md#mcp-servers-in-plugins) travel with their plugin. Installing a plugin is different from copying its server definitions into a personal or workspace configuration.

The connected client's `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json` (or `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`) isn't forwarded to another host or harness. Configure the server in the execution environment or use an eligible forwarded configuration instead. -| Working directory | Yes | No | Yes |
-| Environment file | Yes | No | No |

+| Workspace-root `.mcp.json` | stdio and HTTP | No |

+| Field | Applies to | Purpose |
+|-------|------------|---------|
+| `type` | All servers | `stdio` for a command, `http` for Streamable HTTP, or `sse` for a legacy SSE endpoint. Prefer HTTP when the server supports it. |

+| `tools` | All servers | Tool names to make available. `["*"]` makes all server tools available; use specific names to limit the selection. This doesn't bypass tool approvals. |
+| `oauthClientId` | HTTP and SSE | Client ID for a server that requires a pre-registered OAuth client. This is a flat field, not the editor format's nested `oauth` object. |

+
+### Mask environment variables
+
+In the Copilot harness, use ``chat.agent.sandbox.credentials.envVars`` to protect environment variable values from sandboxed tools. Tools receive placeholders, and the sandbox restores the real values only in HTTPS requests to hosts listed in `injectHosts`.
+
+Enter variable names, not secret values. For example, mask `API_TOKEN` and supply its value only to `api.example.com`:
+
+```json
+{
+    "chat.agent.sandbox.credentials.envVars": {
+        "API_TOKEN": {
+            "injectHosts": ["api.example.com"]
+        }
+    }
+}
+```
+
+On Windows, masking requires [local-network access](#configure-network-access). On Windows and macOS, tools that rely on the operating system's certificate store might also need [sandbox CA certificate trust](#trust-the-sandbox-ca-certificate-on-windows-and-macos).

+For a Windows or macOS remote agent host, use the following CLI workflow on that host. You don't need desktop VS Code or a separate Copilot CLI installation there. For VS Code Insiders, use `code-insiders` instead of `code` in the commands below.
+
+1. Open a terminal that runs on the remote agent-host computer, not the client computer. Use the same OS account as the agent host. If the host sets `COPILOT_HOME`, use the same value.
+
+    Run the commands yourself, not through an agent-executed terminal tool in chat.
+
+1. Create the CA, then add it to the host's OS trust store:
+
+    ```sh
+    code agent sandbox ca create
+    code agent sandbox ca trust
+    ```
+
+1. Accept the CLI confirmation and any required OS authorization. Windows requires administrator approval. macOS might request Keychain authorization.
+
+    If the remote terminal can't complete the authorization prompts, use an interactive login on the host. Do not run the agent host as Administrator or SYSTEM to work around authorization errors.
+
+1. Check that the certificate status is `installed`:
+
+    ```sh
+    code agent sandbox ca status
+    ```
+
+1. Return to the client and select **Refresh** in the certificate notice. The notice disappears when trust is confirmed, without restarting the host or reconnecting. **Refresh** checks certificate status but does not change trust.
+
+If **Refresh** is unavailable, or no certificate notice is visible, restart the remote agent host and reconnect the client after changing trust. Reloading only the client does not reliably clear the host's cached certificate status.
+
+To remove OS trust, run the following commands on the same host with the same OS account and `COPILOT_HOME`. Accept the confirmation and any required OS authorization:
+
+```sh
+code agent sandbox ca remove
+code agent sandbox ca status
+```
+
+The status becomes `notInstalled`. Removal retains the stored CA certificate and private key.

 # Move from the Local to the Copilot harness
 
 The Copilot harness brings the shared coding agent runtime behind Copilot CLI and the [copilot.github_copilot_app_short] into VS Code. Your editor workflows benefit from the same ongoing work on model integration, context efficiency, and tool use as those products. You can work alongside your code in the editor or use the Agents window to supervise tasks across projects.
 
-For organizations, the shared runtime provides a common approach to governing agents across supported clients and development environments. Administrators can manage permissions and sandbox restrictions that the legacy Local harness cannot enforce, while developers use approved tools and services in their workflows.
-
-If you already use agents through the Local harness, this guide helps you make that transition. Review the customizations and integrations your work depends on, continue existing conversations where needed, and verify your organization's controls. The goal is a working setup for your daily tasks, not just a different session target.
+For organizations, the shared runtime provides a common approach to governing agents across supported clients and development environments. Administrators can manage permissions and sandbox restrictions that the legacy Local harness `feature(local-harness)` cannot enforce, while developers use approved tools and services in their workflows.
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> The Local harness `feature(local-harness)` is deprecated and will be removed by **February 2027**. Move your workflows to the Copilot harness before then. The temporary `vscode.temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness` enterprise-managed setting will also be removed.
+
+Use this guide to review the customizations and integrations your work depends on, continue existing conversations where needed, and verify your organization's controls. The goal is a working setup for your daily tasks, not just a different session target.
 
 ## Why move to the Copilot harness

 VS Code uses a permission-based security model where you maintain control over potentially risky operations.
 
-* **Permission levels**: In a Copilot harness session, use the [permissions picker](/docs/agents/run/approvals.md#permission-levels) to choose how tool calls are approved. **Manual permissions** uses your configured approval settings. **Assisted permissions** uses an LLM judge to evaluate each tool call and asks for your approval when the judge does not approve it. **Allow all** auto-approves all tool calls. **Autopilot** is an agent mode that auto-approves all tools and drives the agent to continue working until the task is complete. Available controls depend on the harness and code isolation. For Local harness sessions `feature(local-harness)`, Autopilot is a permission level instead.
 
 * **Terminal approval**: Before executing terminal commands, the agent requests explicit user approval. When terminal auto-approval is enabled, configurable per-command rules (including regex patterns) auto-approve safe commands while prompting for potentially dangerous ones. All subcommands in a compound command must match an approved rule.

-* **Review flow for file changes**: You can [review agent changes](/docs/agents/run/review-code-edits.md) before you commit, merge, or create a pull request. Credentials you explicitly inject, developer-tool configuration and caches, allowed paths, unrestricted or local network access, unsandboxed fallback, and bypass all weaken its isolation. +### Continue a CLI session in VS Code (Experimental)
+
+Move an existing GitHub Copilot CLI conversation from a terminal outside VS Code into the Chat view to continue beside your code without starting over. This workflow requires Copilot CLI 1.0.107 or later and [Copilot harness access](/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses.md#copilot) in VS Code.

-### Troubleshoot Computer Use
-
-* **Computer Use isn't offered**: Check the supported platform and harness, confirm that the setting is on, and restart before starting a new chat. On first use, allow time for the plugin to download.
-* **The agent doesn't ask to turn it on**: The activation prompt isn't shown in Autopilot or chats with automatic replies. Run `/computer on` yourself. If you previously selected **Not Now**, the agent doesn't ask again in that chat.
-* **The macOS setup dialog closes before you finish**: The dialog closes if the waiting tool call ends. Finish granting permissions in System Settings, then ask the agent to retry the task. A new setup card appears if permissions are still missing.
-* **Allow in Settings doesn't open a prompt**: After a restart, macOS might not show a permission prompt it has already shown. Select **Allow in Settings** again to open System Settings.

### [MODIFICADO] `microsoft_vscode-docs::release-notes/v1_146.md`
- **URL Canónica**: https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_146
- **Hash Anterior**: `312773ae2afc8e1113a16484d22c6eb0002f638e6626dfe12cedca0114a9bdb8`
- **Hash Nuevo**: `dda4256b220206be69b63c291e60ddbc1fa950360be484e69e34561d1ebf87da`

```diff
--- microsoft_vscode-docs::release-notes/v1_146.md (prev: 312773ae)
+++ microsoft_vscode-docs::release-notes/v1_146.md (new: dda4256b)
@@ -1,70 +1,348 @@
-**MetaDescription**: Learn what is new in Visual Studio Code Insiders.
+**MetaDescription**: Learn what's new in Visual Studio Code 1.146
 
 # Visual Studio Code 1.146
 
-Follow us on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/showcase/vs-code), [X](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkID=533687), [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/vscode.dev), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/vscode)
+## Release highlights
+
+Save your brainpower for the work that needs it. Inbox mode keeps the right sessions on your radar while agents take on model comparisons. Shape your agent workspace around the task with chat windows and extensions.
+
+* [Inbox mode (Experimental)](#inbox-mode-for-sessions-experimental): Focus on sessions that need your attention across all your projects, and snooze others for later.
+
+* [Model comparison (Preview)](#model-comparison-improvements-preview): Compare results with Copilot Fusion in the mix, or let an agent run comparisons for you.
+
+* [Chat windows (Preview)](#chat-windows-preview): Give chats their own windows and rearrange chats, editors, and terminals to fit the task.
+
+* [Extensions in the Agents window (Experimental)](#install-and-manage-extensions-in-the-agents-window-experimental): Find and install extensions for a richer agent experience.
+
+* [Local harness deprecation](#copilot-harness-and-deprecation-of-the-local-harness): Move to the Copilot harness before the Local harness is removed in February 2027.
+
+Happy coding!
+
+## Agents
+
+### Copilot harness and deprecation of the Local harness
+
+The Copilot harness is our latest agent harness and has been the default for new sessions since [VS Code 1.143](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_143#_copilot-harness-as-the-default). It's built on the Copilot SDK, a shared foundation that helps align behavior, capabilities, and improvements across Copilot products. Copilot harness sessions run through the [Agent Host](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/concepts/agent-host), so you can keep them running in the background and access them from both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window. For organizations, the Copilot harness also enforces managed sandbox and permission policies that the Local harness doesn't.
+
+Thank you to everyone who has shared feedback on using the Copilot harness as your default. Your feedback has shaped the harness experience, and it will continue to guide us through this next step. As of this release, the **Local harness is deprecated and will be removed in three months (February 2027)**:
+
+* **Next three months**: You can still use the Local harness while you move your workflows, but it's functionally frozen. New features and improvements will focus on the Copilot harness and are not guaranteed to be supported by the Local harness.
+* **After three months**: The Local harness will no longer be available. The `vscode.temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness` enterprise-managed setting, introduced in VS Code 1.142 to [keep the Local harness as the default](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/enterprise/manage-ai-settings#_keep-local-harness-as-default), will also be removed.
+
+Because the Copilot harness is already the default for new sessions, you might not need to take any new actions. To confirm you're using the Copilot harness, look for **Copilot** in the harness picker when you start a new session:
+
+![Screenshot showing Copilot selected in the harness picker with a hover description of its Copilot SDK and Agent Host integration.](images/1_146/harness-copilot-description.webp)
+
+If you still use the Local harness, plan to move completely to the Copilot harness before February 2027. The [Local-to-Copilot harness transition guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/move-to-copilot) covers customization compatibility, continuing existing Local conversations, and organization rollout and verification. If you run into any problems, let us know by [filing an issue](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues).
+
+### Inbox mode for sessions (Experimental)
+
+**Setting**: ``sessions.list.inboxEnabled``
+
+Keep track of your agents without checking each workspace. Inbox mode gives you one view of what needs your attention, what's still running, and what's ready to merge.
+
+Enable the ``sessions.list.inboxEnabled`` setting (off by default), and then select **Grouping > Inbox Mode** in the Agents window's sessions list.
+
+![Screenshot showing Inbox Mode selected in the Grouping menu in the Agents window.](images/1_146/sessions-inbox-mode.webp)
+
+Sessions that need your attention appear at the top, above the **Working**, **Ready to merge**, **On hold**, and **Done** groups. If a session can wait, use **Dismiss from Inbox**, **Put on Hold**, or **Snooze** to set it aside. Select **Undo** if you change your mind.
+
+Dismissing a session doesn't archive it. To archive it, select **Mark Session as Done**.
+
+![Screenshot showing sessions needing attention in the Inbox above the Working, Ready to merge, On hold, and Done categories.](images/1_146/sessions-inbox.webp)
+
+### Session list inline actions (Experimental)
+
+**Setting**: ``sessions.list.inlineActions``
+
+Fix failing checks and address review comments directly from the Agents window's sessions list. Enable this setting (off by default) to show inline actions for fixing checks, addressing comments, or both.
+
+Each action sends a request to that row's session or nested session in the background without opening it. The setting does not enable Agent Merge or change action permissions.
+
+![Screenshot showing an Address Comments button beneath a session in the Agents window's sessions list.](images/1_146/inline-session-actions.webp)
+
+### Chat windows (Preview)
+
+**Setting**: ``sessions.chatWindows.enabled``
+
+When several chats run at once, keeping them all in one Agents window means switching between them and losing sight of the one you are waiting on. With chat windows, you can open a chat in a window of its own, and arrange that window so that the chat, its editors, and its terminals fit the task.
+
+To try this preview feature in Stable, enable ``sessions.chatWindows.enabled``. It is enabled by default in VS Code Insiders, and off by default in Stable.
+
+Learn more about [chat windows](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/agents-window#_open-chats-in-separate-windows) in our documentation.
+
+To open a chat in a new window, right-click the session or chat in the sessions list and select **Open in** > **New Window**. You can also drag a chat out of the Agents window to create a new window. You can move it back with the **Move to Main Window** command.
+
+A chat window can hold several chats from one or more sessions: pick another session in its title bar, drag a chat in from another window, or select **New Session** (``Shortcut: sessions.chatWindow.newSession``) at the left of the title bar to start a new session in that window. Chat windows reopen with their chats and editors after you restart VS Code.
+
+The content within a chat window is organized into parts, which you can arrange freely to fit your workflow.
+
+<video src="images/1_146/chat-windows.mp4" title="Video showing moving a chat into a new window and arranging parts in a chat window." autoplay loop controls muted></video>
+
+* **Move parts:** Drag a part by the grabber on the top edge of its card to another side of the window, or beside another part. You can also use **Move Part Left**, **Move Part Right**, **Move Part Up**, and **Move Part Down**.
+* **Move tabs between parts:** Drag a tab to another part, or drop it on a part's edge to split that part. Use **Move Editor to Part** or **Move Editor into New Part Left/Right/Above/Below** to do the same from the Command Palette. Drag an editor tab onto the chat input to attach it to the chat as context.
+* **Place the terminal:** Dragging the terminal under the editor or under the chat sets **Terminal Position** to **Under Editor** or **Under Chat**. Dropping it on the bottom edge of the window sets **Full Width**. You can also change the position from the **...** menu of the terminal.
+* **Switch the layout:** Use **Configure Layout** in the title bar to show the chat, the editor, or both, side by side or stacked. In the stacked layout, **Agents: Toggle Chat Conversation** collapses the chat to only its input, so the editor takes the rest of the window.
+
+Use **Developer: Reset Chat Window Layout** to return a window to how it first opened.
+
+Let us know what you think by [filing an issue](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues).
+
+### Install and manage extensions in the Agents window (Experimental)
+
+The **Extensions** section of Agent Customizations lets you choose which installed extensions run in the Agents window without changing their enablement in editor windows. Previously, adding an extension meant switching to an editor window to install it. In this release, you can find, install, and uninstall extensions without leaving the Agents window:
+
+* **Install from the Marketplace**: Searching also queries the Marketplace and lists matching extensions that you don't have yet, with their publisher, install count, and rating. Installing an extension adds it to VS Code and enables it in the Agents window. To install a different version, such as a pre-release, use the dropdown next to **Install**.
+* **Know what won't work before installing**: Extensions that contribute views, debuggers, status bar items, or walkthroughs without declaring support for the Agents window show a warning that lists the unsupported features. Extensions that can't be installed, for example because your organization doesn't allow them, show the reason.
+* **Open with a keyboard shortcut**: Press ``Shortcut: workbench.view.extensions`` or run **Extensions: Manage Extensions** to open the section. If you changed the shortcut for the Extensions view in editor windows, your shortcut also works in the Agents window.
+
+![Screenshot showing the Extensions section in the Agents window.](images/1_146/extensions-agents-window.webp)
+
+### Model comparison improvements (Preview)
+
+**Setting**: ``sessions.chat.compareAgents.tools.enabled``
+
+[Compare Models](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/compare-models) in the Agents window lets you run the same prompt across models, evaluate their results with a judge, and combine their strengths with a synthesizer. This release makes comparisons easier to configure, organize, and automate:
+
+* **Judge and synthesize chat-only responses**: Add a judge and synthesizer without selecting a workspace. Synthesis starts when you select **Synthesize** and creates a new chat without changing the original attempts.
+* **Compare Copilot Fusion**: Select Fusion and its supported effort tiers for an attempt, the judge, or the synthesizer.
+* **Let an agent run evaluations (Experimental)**: Enable ``sessions.chat.compareAgents.tools.enabled`` to let agents discover models, launch comparisons, and read results and conversation references to summarize findings across scenarios. The tools are off by default and require Compare Models to be enabled. Disabling them still leaves manual comparisons available.
+
+### Canvases improvements (Preview)
+
+**Setting**: ``chat.canvases.enabled``
+
+[Canvases](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/canvases) are shared, interactive surfaces where you and Copilot work together on plans, dashboards, and other artifacts. This release adds permission prompts and improves canvas discovery and continuity:
```

 # Ruby on Rails
+
+## Version and Application Context
+
+- Read `Gemfile.lock`, `config.load_defaults`, and environment configuration before choosing APIs or changing infrastructure. Preserve the application's supported Rails and Ruby versions.
+- New Rails 8 applications default to Propshaft and include production configuration for Solid Queue, Solid Cache, and Solid Cable. Existing apps may retain other asset, job, cache, or cable backends; inspect environment-specific configuration before suggesting a migration.
+- On Rails 8+, `bin/rails generate authentication` provides a starting point for session-based authentication and password resets. Use it only when it fits the requested authentication work; review authorization and any additional account requirements separately.
+
+References: [Rails 8.0 release notes](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/8_0_release_notes.html), [Active Job configuration](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_job_basics.html), [Rails authentication guidance](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/security.html).
 
 ## General Guidelines
 
@@ -12,8 +20,7 @@
 - Apply the Single Responsibility Principle to classes, methods, and modules.
 - Prefer composition over inheritance; extract reusable logic into modules or services.
 - Keep controllers thin — move business logic into models, services, or command/query objects.
-- Apply the “fat model, skinny controller” pattern thoughtfully and with clean abstractions.
-- Extract business logic into service objects for reusability and testability.
+- Keep model responsibilities focused; extract a service or query object when an actual workflow or reuse boundary justifies it.
 - Use partials or view components to reduce duplication and simplify views.
 - Use `unless` for negative conditions, but avoid it with `else` for clarity.
 - Avoid deeply nested conditionals — favor guard clauses and method extractions.
@@ -42,7 +49,7 @@
 
 ## App Directory Structure
 
-- Define service objects in the `app/services` directory to encapsulate business logic.
+- Put service objects in `app/services` when needed; do not create extra application layers by default.
 - Use form objects located in `app/forms` to manage validation and submission logic.
 - Implement JSON serializers in the `app/serializers` directory to format API responses.
 - Define authorization policies in `app/policies` to control user access to resources.
@@ -84,7 +91,7 @@
 
 ## Frontend Development Best Practices
 
-- Use `app/javascript` as the main directory for managing JavaScript packs, modules, and frontend logic in Rails 6+ with Webpacker or esbuild.
+- Use the application's existing JavaScript setup under `app/javascript`. Modern Rails supports import maps or JavaScript bundling; follow the configured approach rather than introducing Webpacker. See [Working with JavaScript in Rails](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/working_with_javascript_in_rails.html).
 - Structure your JavaScript by components or domains, not by file types, to keep things modular.
 - Leverage Hotwire (Turbo + Stimulus) for real-time updates and minimal JavaScript in Rails-native apps.
 - Use Stimulus controllers for binding behavior to HTML and managing UI logic declaratively.

 ## Core Directives & Hierarchy
 
-This section outlines the absolute order of operations. These rules have the highest priority and must not be violated.
+These instructions guide scope and communication within the user's request. Follow applicable system, platform, and repository rules, including tool permissions and security requirements.
 
-1.  **Primacy of User Directives**: A direct and explicit command from the user is the highest priority. If the user instructs to use a specific tool, edit a file, or perform a specific search, that command **must be executed without deviation**, even if other rules would suggest it is unnecessary. All other instructions are subordinate to a direct user order.
+1.  **User-Directed Scope**: Follow the user's requested outcome within the applicable rules and available permissions. Complete the necessary edits and verification; when an action is unavailable or outside the authorized scope, explain the limitation.
 2.  **Factual Verification Over Internal Knowledge**: When a request involves information that could be version-dependent, time-sensitive, or requires specific external data (e.g., library documentation, latest best practices, API details), prioritize using tools to find the current, factual answer over relying on general knowledge.
 3.  **Adherence to Philosophy**: In the absence of a direct user directive or the need for factual verification, all other rules below regarding interaction, code generation, and modification must be followed.
 
 ## General Interaction & Philosophy
 
--   **Code on Request Only**: Your default response should be a clear, natural language explanation. Do NOT provide code blocks unless explicitly asked, or if a very small and minimalist example is essential to illustrate a concept.  Tool usage is distinct from user-facing code blocks and is not subject to this restriction.
+-   **Match the Request**: Answer explanatory questions clearly and concisely. Treat requests to implement or fix behavior as authorization to make the necessary code changes and verify them; do not require the user to separately ask for code.
 -   **Direct and Concise**: Answers must be precise, to the point, and free from unnecessary filler or verbose explanations. Get straight to the solution without "beating around the bush".
 -   **Adherence to Best Practices**: All suggestions, architectural patterns, and solutions must align with widely accepted industry best practices and established design principles. Avoid experimental, obscure, or overly "creative" approaches. Stick to what is proven and reliable.
 -   **Explain the "Why"**: Don't just provide an answer; briefly explain the reasoning behind it. Why is this the standard approach? What specific problem does this pattern solve? This context is more valuable than the solution itself.
@@ -20,7 +20,7 @@
 -   **Principle of Simplicity**: Always provide the most straightforward and minimalist solution possible. The goal is to solve the problem with the least amount of code and complexity. Avoid premature optimization or over-engineering.
 -   **Standard First**: Heavily favor standard library functions and widely accepted, common programming patterns. Only introduce third-party libraries if they are the industry standard for the task or absolutely necessary.
 -   **Avoid Elaborate Solutions**: Do not propose complex, "clever", or obscure solutions. Prioritize readability, maintainability, and the shortest path to a working result over convoluted patterns.
--   **Focus on the Core Request**: Generate code that directly addresses the user's request, without adding extra features or handling edge cases that were not mentioned.
+-   **Focus on the Core Request**: Generate code that directly addresses the user's request without adding extra features. Retain validation, error handling, and edge cases needed for correctness, security, and the requested behavior.
 
 ## Surgical Code Modification
